newsitem.title: USA: GM October sales seen down, while total industry rises.
newsitem.headline: GM October sales seen down, while total industry rises.

text.p: General Motors Corp.'s U.S. car and light truck sales in October are expected to dip only slightly because hefty inventories kept sales moving despite a three-week strike by Canadian autoworkers, analysts said.

October sales for the full industry are expected to rise between 4 percent and 6 percent on a daily selling basis, they said. The percentage is based on 27 selling days in October, versus 26 in the year-ago month.

Estimates for the seasonally adjusted annual selling rate for light vehicles were running in the low- to mid-15 million range, according to analysts. However, the actual sales pace for October will be less than that, cautioned Michael Luckey, president of Luckey Consulting.
That is because the numbers provided by the U.S. Commerce Department to compute the seasonal rate artificially add between 300,000 to 400,000 units to the sales total, Luckey said.

A monthly selling rate of 15.1 million would show that American consumers are continuing to buy cars and light trucks at a healthy rate, said George Magliano, an analyst at WEFA Group, an industry consulting firm.
"I had expected weakness by now and obviously it hasn't shown up," he said. "Obviously, the consumer is still there, still buying and the industry is still very healthy."
The seasonally adjusted rate for September was 15.02 million, and 14.22 million in October 1995, when a strike by the car haulers union held back new vehicle deliveries.
GM is scheduled to report its sales on Friday. Analysts said GM experienced a double-digit drop in car sales, but a jump in sales of pickups, sport/utilities and minivans by about the same amount.

Lehman Brothers analyst Joseph Phillippi said GM continued to have poor performances from its Oldsmobile, Buick and Cadillac divisions. The company has previously blamed its slow car sales on the fact that consumers are waiting for many of the automaker's 15 new vehicle models to hit showrooms before buying a new car.
"They're still struggling through with a lot of old iron," Phillippi said.

At the end of September, according to the most recent figures available, GM had more than a 60 days' supply of vehicles on dealer lots from many of the car lines affected by the 20-day Canadian walkout. The industry generally considers a 60-day supply to be ideal.

GM's November sales, however, could be hurt by the ongoing plant shutdowns associated with the Canadian walkout and local strikes in Janesville, Wis., and Indianapolis, Phillippi said. The U.S. strikes, if they last for a long period, could cause a severe drop in dealer inventories of GM's popular full-size pickup trucks and sport/utility vehicles.
Chrysler Corp., also scheduled to report Friday, will post another month of double-digit increases in both cars and light truck sales, analysts said.
"They are having a blockbuster runaway October," Phillippi said.

Ford Motor Co., which stepped up cash rebates on its Taurus sedan in late September and even included the first-ever rebate on 1997 Taurus models, will also post gains, but not as high as Chrysler's, analysts said.
Burnham Securities Inc. analyst David Healy said sales of domestically produced Ford cars were unchanged in October, while light truck sales climbed 9 percent.
Ford is scheduled to report its October sales on Nov. 5.
